The group People Not Politicians submitted the appeal on Wednesday, a day after U.S. District Court Chief Justice Stephen Clark ruled that Missouri can and should use the new map. Clark said that the state already voted using the map in the Aug. 4 primary, and tossing it would disenfranchise voters forced to elect lawmakers from primaries they couldn’t vote in.
Hoskins said in a statement that, with Kavanaugh’s decision, he’s directing election officials to use the 2022 map.
People Not Politicians Executive Director Richard von Glahn said in a statement that the decision left Missouri voters in charge of which maps should be implemented. His group gathered more than 300,000 signatures to appear on the November ballot. Hoskins previously decertified the petition, but the Missouri high court ruled on Sept. 3 that the referendum must appear on the ballot.
“Missourians don’t need a Secretary of State who manufactures confusion; they need one who follows the law,” von Glahn said.
University at Buffalo Assistant Professor of Politics Shawn Donahue told Straight Arrow that Kavanaugh’s ruling is still complicated as it pauses Clark’s order while the lawsuit is appealed in the Eighth Circuit Court of Appeals. The court rejected an appeal Wednesday due to lack of jurisdiction and proof of harm.
“It seems at first glance that SCOTUS does not seem to want to have lower federal courts disturb the Missouri Supreme Court ruling,” he wrote.
Donahue expects Missouri will take an aggressive approach in the appellate court knowing the three-judge panel was appointed by Republican presidents. He added that Kavanaugh did send the application to the full court, but didn’t note any dissents.
“But for now, it would seem to put the 2022 map back as the map that will be used,” Donahue wrote. “A big question is still who the candidates will be for the general election.”

sources.text:
(The Center Square) – The U.S. Supreme Court on Thursday again rejected a Missouri congressional map that would give Republicans an advantage ahead of the midterm elections.
Justices on the high court granted a requst to block a lower court decision that would have allowed the redrawn congressional map to remain in place. Justice Brett Kavanaugh denied the request after blocking the map’s implementation on Monday but allowed respondents in the case a chance to petition the court for certiorari.
Missouri redrew its congressional maps in 2025 and held a primary with the newly proposed maps which could give Republicans one additional congressional seat in the state.
“The district court’s legally baseless [order] must not be permitted to detonate in the middle of Missouri’s congressional elections to blow up the clear and careful ruling of the Missouri Supreme Court and the fundamental rights of Missouri voters,” lawyer’s for the advocacy group People Not Politicans wrote to the high court.
Missouri Secretary of State Denny Hoskins said the high court’s denial of redawn congressional maps would cause unnecessary chaos before the November general election.
“It would be extraordinarily burdensome to change Missouri’s congressional map with the Primary Election having been completed,” lawyers for Hoskins wrote in a brief to the high court.
The previous maps, adopted in 2022, favor Republicans by a margin of 6-2 insetead of the newly drawn maps that could give a 7-1 advantage for the GOP. Candidates across the state will likely be in slightly altered districts for the general election.
Kavanaugh invited those involved in the case to petition the high court. If a petition is granted, justices on the court could hear arguments in the case during its upcoming term.
The Supreme Court has already scheduled arguments through the remainder of the calendar year. The Missouri case, with its implications for the midterm elections, will likely not be solved by that point.

Supreme Court blocks Missouri from using new map favoring GOP in midterm elections
sources.text:
Supreme Court blocks Missouri from using new map favoring GOP in midterm elections
The Supreme Court on Thursday temporarily blocked Missouri from using a newly drawn congressional map that favors Republicans in this year's midterm elections.
In an unsigned order with no noted dissents, the Supreme Court said that Missouri Secretary of State Denny Hoskins must use a 2022 congressional map in the November elections, not a new congressional map that would favor Republicans and could eliminate a seat held by Democrats.
Missouri currently has six Republicans and two Democrats in its U.S. House delegation, and the new map targets one of the Democratic seats, which could result in a 7-1 split favoring Republicans. The proposed map targeted the seat of longtime Rep. Emanuel Cleaver.
The decision, for now, blocks a lower court decision by Missouri U.S. District Judge Stephen Clark, who said Tuesday that the new map must be used. Late Thursday, Clark refused to stay his order, and a panel of judges on the Eight Circuit Court of Appeals is currently overseeing an appeal of his order.
The justices did not say why they blocked the new map.
Minutes before the high court's order, lawyers for Hoskins and Missouri said in a filing with the court that it would be "extraordinarily burdensome" to change the congressional map after the state's August primary elections were held using the new, Republican-created map. The state said that the legal challenge was "seeking to destabilize" the state's midterm elections, and risked the "disenfranchisement of hundreds of thousands of voters."
Earlier this week, Justice Brett Kavanaugh rejected an appeal from Hoskins, and sided with Missouri's Supreme Court, which said last week that the new districts cannot be used in the November midterms.
The Missouri Supreme Court unanimously ruled in favor of challengers to the new map, ordering the statewide vote they requested. Missouri's highest court said a petition circulated by a group called People Not Politicians that demanded a statewide vote before the congressional map was implemented superseded the new map.
The new map was enacted by Missouri Republicans last year as part of a nationwide redistricting effort undertaken by President Trump and Republicans to hold the slim GOP House majority in Congress. Similar redistricting efforts were undertaken in Texas and North Carolina by Republicans, and in California by Democrats. A voter-approved ballot initiative to redraw Virginia's map to be more favorable to Democrats was rebuffed by the state's Supreme Court.

sources.news_title: U.S. Supreme Court blocks Republican-drawn congressional map in Missouri
sources.text: The U.S. Supreme Court blocked Missouri on Thursday from using a redrawn congressional map that favors Republicans in November’s midterm elections, dealing a setback to U.S President Donald Trump and the party’s odds of maintaining its slim majority in the House of Representatives. The justices granted an emergency request by the map’s challengers to suspend a federal judge’s decision that allowed only the reconfigured boundaries to be used in the Nov. 3 elections. The court’s brief order was unsigned and gave no explanation, as is common when the justices handle emergency matters. No justice publicly dissented from the decision. The challengers, including a group opposed to the Republican-drawn map called People Not Politicians, had swiftly sought the Supreme Court’s intervention after St. Louis, Missouri-based Chief U.S. District Judge Stephen Clark issued his decision on Tuesday. Clark’s decision came shortly after the Supreme Court had declined to intervene in a separate bid by Missouri officials to reinstate the redrawn map, which the state’s top court had blocked until it is put to a referendum. The judge’s order appeared to conflict with the Missouri Supreme Court’s unanimous September 3 ruling blocking the map, leaving the state’s congressional districts in limbo and injecting further confusion into the high-stakes electoral fight. Missouri Republicans adopted the new map, which dismantled the Kansas City-based seat of longtime Democratic Representative Emanuel Cleaver, in 2025 as part of a broader effort backed by President Donald Trump to redraw congressional districts in ways that could benefit Republican candidates. Republicans hold a narrow 219-214 majority in the U.S. House, including one independent who caucuses with Republicans. Reporting by Andrew Chung; Editing by Chizu Nomiyama

sources.news_title: Terse Supreme Court ruling shuts down GOP's Missouri gerrymander hopes for midterms
sources.text:
The U.S. Supreme Court on Thursday blocked a federal judge's order forcing Missouri to hold its November elections under a gerrymandered map the state's high court said never took effect.
The order ran roughly ten lines, carried no signature and offered no reasoning. Justice Brett Kavanaugh, who handles emergency appeals from Missouri, referred the application to the full court, which granted it with no noted dissents.
The stay freezes the lower court's Sept. 8 order while the case moves through the 8th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals and any further appeal to the justices, the order said.
That leaves Missouri with the congressional map it used in 2022 and 2024 for the Nov. 3 election, Election Law Blog reported.
The difference is one seat in the U.S. House. The 2022 lines produced a delegation of six Republicans and two Democrats, while the 2025 replacement was drawn to give Republicans seven of the state's eight districts.
At the center of the fight is House Bill 1, the mid-decade redraw Missouri Republicans passed in 2025 with backing from President Donald Trump, the Missouri Independent reported.
It worked mainly by reshaping the Kansas City-based 5th District. Rep. Emanuel Cleaver (D-MO) holds that seat, according to the Missouri Independent. Opponents turned to a provision of the Missouri Constitution that lets voters veto a legislative act, Democracy Docket reported.
The group People Not Politicians submitted more than 300,000 signatures last December. That forced a statewide referendum on the new districts, Democracy Docket said.
The Missouri Supreme Court ruled unanimously on Sept. 3 that because those signatures arrived before the new districts took effect, House Bill 1 never became law.
Chief U.S. District Judge Stephen Clark, a Trump appointee in St. Louis, ordered the opposite on Tuesday, barring Missouri from using any map except House Bill 1, according to Democracy Docket.
That map had already governed Missouri's August primary, KOMU reported.
The lawsuit before Clark was filed by Rep. Bob Onder (R-MO), state Sen. Rick Brattin (R-MO) and two voters, the Associated Press reported. Brattin won the Republican primary in Cleaver's reshaped district, according to the Missouri Independent.
Clark found that switching districts between the primary and the general election would likely violate the Equal Protection Clause, the constitutional promise that voters be treated alike, KCUR reported.
"Using a different map for the general election would wreak havoc on the fairness and orderliness of Missouri's congressional elections, calling into question the candidacy of those nominated in the primaries and the votes of those who voted in the primaries," Clark wrote, according to the Associated Press. "Widespread voter confusion would inevitably follow."
The referendum reaches voters as Proposition A on Nov. 3, the Missouri Independent reported.
If they approve it, the 2025 districts take effect 30 days later and can be used in future elections.

sources.news_title: US Supreme Court delivers another massive blow to Missouri Republicans
sources.text:
Missouri Republicans have already lost several of its lawsuits as part of the ongoing effort to change the congressional maps less than two months before the 2026 election. Now they're facing another blow. 
"Law Dork" Chris Geidner posted on BlueSky that the U.S. Supreme Court has weighed in again on the temporary restraining order a federal district court issued blocking changes to the electoral maps. 
It has been a tough road for Missouri Secretary of State Denny Hoskins, a Republican, who got a ruling from the state Supreme Court blocking the maps. He then ran to the United States District Court for the Eastern District of Missouri, demanding that they step in. They did, and Hoskins decided that the district court superseded the state Supreme Court. A law school professor explained that that isn't how it works. 
Hoskins on Tuesday emailed election officials, instructing them to break the law and use the map the court ruled against. His email prompted the state Supreme Court to ask why it shouldn't hold Hoskins in contempt of court for defying its ruling. Hoskins had until noon on Wednesday to submit an excuse to the Missouri high court, but instead, he begged the district court to step in and protect him. 
In the early morning hours of Thursday, they released a ruling saying that they would not. 
The only higher court that can overrule the state Supreme Court is the U.S. Supreme Court, and in its ruling, it made it clear that it deferred to the state Supreme Court. 
Hoskins rushed to the U.S. Supreme Court again — but on Thursday morning, they struck it down once again.

sources.news_title: Supreme Court blocks Missouri’s use of GOP-favored congressional map

sources.text:
Election officials in Missouri are now planning to send out midterm ballots to voters for their old Congressional districts, after the U.S. Supreme Court intervened in the state's long-running court battle over a new map used in primaries last month.
Earlier Thursday, the High Court granted an emergency appeal blocking the Republican-backed 2025 redistricting map that would reshape the state's eight House districts, just two days after Justice Brett Kavanaugh declined to hear an appeal from state officials.
The case, centered on the replacement for the 2022 map, has passed through multiple courts, including the Missouri Supreme Court, leaving officials uncertain which map they would use for the November election.
"When we saw that the Supreme Court of the United States declined to hear an appeal of the Supreme Court of Missouri's directive, we were good for about 10 minutes," Boone County Clerk Brianna Lennon told Newsweek Thursday afternoon, referring to the near immediate follow-up to Kavanaugh's denial from the Eastern District of Missouri ordering the new map be used.
"So, we knew that there would be a number of appeals and everyone at that point, I think, really kind of found themselves in a position of just waiting," Lennon said. "There was no reason to create ballots that we would have to redo. So we were cautiously optimistic that we would get some sort of resolution from the courts before we would have to create ballots to be sent out to our military and overseas voters, which is next week, September 18th."
The Supreme Court's actions led experts Newsweek spoke to to one conclusion about the debate: the midterms would use the 2022 map.
"This case is now effectively over," Justin Levitt, a law professor at Loyola Law School, told Newsweek following the case. "The Supreme Court’s stay puts the 2022 map back on the ballot (as it should have been) for the fall elections."
"Good for the Court!" Vikram Amar, Daniel J. Dykstra endowed chair and distinguished professor of law at UC Davis School of Law, told Newsweek following the ruling.
Newsweek reached out to Missouri Secretary of State Denny Hoskins for comment Thursday morning.
The second appeal to the U.S. Supreme Court over the issue came from the new map's challengers, People Not Politicians, a group that sought a referendum on the plan.
In a statement shared with Newsweek Thursday, Richard von Glahn, executive director of the group, said, "The law is the law, the Missouri constitution is clear as was the Missouri Supreme Court. Over 305,000 Missouri voters—Republicans, Democrats and Independents took action to block this political power grab last fall. People, not politicians, will have the final say when they vote NO on Proposition A this November."
Supreme Court Prevents Use of Redistricting Maps in Midterms: What We Know
The Supreme Court's decision to hear the case and grant a stay came Thursday morning, hours before Hoskins was due to appear in state court over allegations of contempt.
People Not Politicians, which successfully challenged Missouri's 2025 congressional map in state court, argued that the federal district court improperly overrode the Missouri Supreme Court's ruling that a referendum petition suspended the map.
The group told the Supreme Court that Missouri election officials should follow state law and use the older 2022 map in November, arguing that neither the Equal Protection Clause nor Article I, Section 2 guarantees voters the right to remain in the same congressional district for both primary and general elections.
It also said the federal court's order created election chaos by requiring use of a map that Missouri's highest court had ruled "is not the law and never has been the law."
Hoskins and the state, meanwhile, had argued that switching back to the 2022 map after the August primary would violate the constitutional rights of hundreds of thousands of voters.
They said many Missourians would be forced to vote in the general election for candidates they had no opportunity to help nominate in the primary, while election officials were already printing ballots under the 2025 map.
The United States, supporting Missouri, made similar arguments and said changing maps between the primary and general election would create "two classes of voters" because some voters would remain in the same district while others would be moved into different ones, depriving them of a full role in choosing the member of Congress who will represent them.
The Justice Department also argued that People Not Politicians likely lacked standing to pursue the appeal.
Later Thursday, the Missouri Supreme Court found Hoskins in contempt when he failed to comply with its redistricting ruling. He then ordered election officials to use the old map.
"Following the United States Supreme Court’s stay, the only governing court order in effect is from the Missouri Supreme Court," Hoskins said in a brief statement shared online. "In accordance with that order, my Office is directing local election authorities to use the 2022 congressional map."
New Missouri Redistricting Map Explained
The debate centers on whether Missouri should use its 2022 congressional map or the districts Republicans redrew last year. The newer map could give the GOP seven of Missouri’s eight House seats, rather than six, and was used in the August primaries.
The Missouri legislature approved House Bill 1 in September 2025, replacing the congressional map the state had enacted in 2022. The measure passed comfortably in both chambers before Republican Governor Michael Kehoe signed it into law. Missouri then used the new map during its August 2026 primary elections, in which approximately 1.2 million voters cast ballots.
On September 3, the Missouri Supreme Court ruled that the referendum was valid and said the petition suspended HB 1, ordering state officials to return to the state's previous 2022 congressional map for the November election.
The following day, a group of congressional candidates and voters sued in federal court, arguing that switching maps after the primary would violate the constitutional rights of voters who had already nominated candidates under the HB 1 districts. A federal judge agreed and temporarily blocked Missouri from abandoning the 2025 map.
After the Eighth Circuit declined to intervene, People Not Politicians asked the U.S. Supreme Court to step in.
Missouri Officials Prepare for the Midterms
In Boone County, a Democratic-leaning area of roughly 190,000 residents that backed Kamala Harris over President Donald Trump by about 54 percent to 44 percent in the 2024 presidential election, efforts are now underway in earnest to prepare for November 3.
Lennon told Newsweek that the back-and-forth over the maps had given her runway to prepare for either outcome.
"We knew that it would be a kind of last-minute decision about what ballots we were going to be using because of all of these court cases, but we had to deal with this in August when we were preparing for the primary, so it's not like this is the first time it's happened this year," she said.
"Which, unfortunately, makes it so that we have some practice with having to do this in a rushed manner. But it gave us some practice and, that way, I feel confident that we can get ballots in the hands of voters and they can feel confident in making their voice heard."
Lennon said she had her team create the new database for the 2025 districts, while keeping the 2022 files on hand in case, telling Newsweek, "it is simply a switch that we need to know which way to flip it."
What Happens Next
The Supreme Court's order is temporary and does not fully resolve the underlying dispute over the congressional map Missouri must use in the future.
The justices granted a stay of the federal district court's restraining order while they consider the appeal brought by People Not Politicians, meaning Missouri cannot currently rely on the lower court's directive to use the 2025 HB 1 map.
Levitt told Newsweek that he believed the stay would remain through the midterm election.
"In the fall, voters will vote on HB1, the mid-decade gerrymander," he said. "If the voters approve it, it will govern congressional elections going forward after 2026. If the voters reject it, it’s dead.
"Either way, there’s no federal case remaining—the premise of the federal case was entirely based on a general election under different lines than the primary-and so that case will be moot after the 2026 elections, at which point the Supreme Court case will disappear."
Whether the court decides to let the case peter out or if a formal hearing will be scheduled remains to be seen. For now, the 2022 map takes over for the midterms.
For Lennon, she believes the case has at least led to higher voter engagement, with voters now set to have a say on the map as well as a number of state Constitutional amendments.
"I think people were already set to be engaged in this election and now that they're getting a full view behind the curtain of what goes into making an election successful," she said. "I think it's really been beneficial for voter education."

The one-paragraph decision will affect only a single seat, however, it is an unusual election-related loss for Republicans at the 6-3 conservative Supreme Court. And it undercuts President Donald Trump’s effort to eke an advantage out of state congressional maps across the country to retain Republican control of the House next year.
“The law is the law, the Missouri constitution is clear as was the Missouri Supreme Court,” said Richard von Glahn, executive director of People Not Politicians Missouri, the group that challenged the map and filed the emergency appeal at the Supreme Court. “Over 305,000 Missouri voters — Republicans, Democrats and independents — took action to block this political power grab last fall.”
Aides to Missouri Attorney General Catherine Hanaway, a Republican, did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Even without the seat they sought to gain in Missouri, Republicans have still drawn nine more seats in their favor than Democrats have, according to a CNN analysis. That could be a bulwark for the GOP as it tries to hold onto House control facing major headwinds in Trump’s unpopularity and national concerns about the economy and cost of living.
That doesn’t mean the GOP will gain nine seats this fall due to redistricting. Democrats believe they can still hold onto several of the seats drawn to Republican advantage, particularly in districts with significant Latino populations that shifted to the right during Trump’s 2024 victory but have shown signs of moving back toward the left.
People Not Politicians, organized a campaign to put the new GOP-friendly map to a referendum after the state legislature approved the map last year. Missouri’s highest court had backed that effort last week, effectively requiring the state to revert to an earlier map. And when state officials appealed that ruling to the US Supreme Court last week, Justice Brett Kavanaugh declined to review it.
That decision, it turned out, wasn’t the end of the dispute. Minutes after Kavanaugh issued a brief one-sentence order, a federal judge in Missouri reviewing a different case handed down a temporary order that effectively pushed state officials back to the map that advantaged the GOP. Missouri Secretary of State Denny Hoskins, a Republican, said the state would proceed with the GOP map.
People Not Politicians filed a flurry of appeals seeking to pause that order from US District Judge Stephen Clark, a Trump nominee. And on Wednesday evening, the case returned to the US Supreme Court.

It’s not clear why the Supreme Court sided with People Not Politicians, but critics noted that much of the dispute around the second map involved questions of state and not federal law.
The Supreme Court’s conservative majority — and Kavanaugh, in particular — have frequently also cited a legal doctrine known as the “Purcell principle” that warns federal courts against ruling in election cases that could change the status quo right before an election.

The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the U.S. Supreme Court decision.
Missouri’s highest court scrutinizes secretary of state’s actions
Earlier Thursday, Missouri’s top court convened a hearing on whether to hold Republican Secretary of State Denny Hoskins in contempt for not following its orders to use the districts passed after the last census. Hoskins had instead told local election authorities to use the new Trump-backed map, pointing to a competing order from a federal judge on Tuesday that forbade him from using anything other than the new districts.
Missouri Supreme Court judges, while questioning a state attorney representing Hoskins, repeatedly pressed for Hoskins to send out guidance Thursday to use the 2022 version of the congressional districts.
“We’re in a precarious situation,” Chief Justice W. Brent Powell said.
Hoskins later released a statement acknowledging the U.S. Supreme Court decision, saying “my Office is directing local election authorities to use the 2022 congressional map.”
The court then reconvened, finding Hoskins in contempt for violating its order not to use the Trump-backed map but then quickly declaring that he had corrected the problem with his latest order to use the 2022 map. The court imposed no consequences on Hoskins.
Missouri voters could face significantly different districts
Outside the court, progressive activist Keith Rose stood in the rain protesting Hoskins’ legal maneuverings to try to use the Trump-backed map. Rose, who helped gather petition signatures to put the new map to a statewide vote, said he hopes the U.S. Supreme Court’s decision Thursday ends the uncertainty.
“We need some finality. We need to focus on the real issues that Missourians care about,” Rose said.
Candidates who won Missouri’s August primary already have been certified for the November ballot according to the number of the district they won. But those districts could substantially change shape.
The 5th Congressional District encompasses only the Kansas City area under the 2022 map that Republican lawmakers passed after the last census. Under the revised map backed by Trump, portions are shed to neighboring districts and the remainder is stretched into rural Republican areas. About 59% of the potential voters are new to the district under that version, according to an AP estimate.
Some other states that have switched congressional districts after their primaries have redone their primary votes. Alabama held a new primary in August under revised districts when the U.S. Supreme Court allowed a change to occur after voting in the original May primary.
In Missouri’s case, however, no court has suggested redoing the primary.
The redistricting battle began over a year ago
Missouri’s battle over its congressional districts has spanned more than a year and spawned confusion over which districts will be in place for voters.
It was the second Republican-led state, after Texas, to enact new districts after Trump urged Republicans last year to redraw House districts to their advantage ahead of the midterm elections.
The revised districts target a Kansas City-based seat held by Democratic Rep. Emanuel Cleaver of Kansas City, aiming to help Republicans win seven of the state’s eight House seats in the midterm elections.
Redistricting opponents collected hundreds of thousands of petition signatures seeking to force a statewide vote on the new districts. They submitted the signatures in December. But Hoskins waited until August — on the same day as Missouri’s primary — to reject the petition. Hoskins asserted that a referendum petition could not be used for congressional redistricting.
The delay allowed Missouri to use the new districts in its August primary. Cleaver was unopposed for the Democratic nomination. State Sen. Rick Brattin won the Republican primary for the right to challenge Cleaver. Brattin was among those suing in federal court to try to prevent the state from reverting to the prior districts.
Republican U.S. Rep. Bob Onder, who was also among those suing, said Thursday: “This isn’t over.” He noted that the 8th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals will hear arguments on the merits of his case.
Republican state officials have argued that it would violate voters’ federal rights to switch districts before the general election.
But the Missouri Supreme Court last week ordered Hoskins to put the redistricting referendum on the November ballot, which he did. It also ruled that the new districts never became law and instead were suspended retroactively to the December petition submission. The court barred Hoskins from using the new map and said the old map — passed by Republican lawmakers in 2022 after the last census — must be used in the November election.
The state then appealed to the U.S. Supreme Court to block the state court decision. Justice Brett Kavanaugh rejected the request.
The group People Not Politicians Missouri, which sponsored the redistricting referendum, applauded the Supreme Court decisions that left the state court ruling in place.
“The law is the law, the Missouri constitution is clear as was the Missouri Supreme Court,” said Executive Director Richard von Glahn. “The courts have settled this, now it’s up to Missouri voters to finish the job and vote NO on Proposition A.”
Whitehurst reported from Washington. Associated Press journalist Hannah Recht contributed from Washington.

sources.news_title: The Latest: US Supreme Court again rejects push to use Trump-backed congressional map in Missouri
sources.text:
The U.S. Supreme Court again rejected a push to use Missouri congressional maps backed by President Donald Trump on Thursday, a loss for Republicans trying to maintain control of the House in the fast-approaching midterm elections. The decision means Missouri will run the general election with a different congressional map than was used in the primary.
Also, Trump has pledged to send every American adult $5,000 if Republicans retain control of the House and Senate in the midterm elections. The dubious promise would likely cost more than $1 trillion and require congressional approval, and would further exacerbate the country’s nearly $1.8 trillion annual budget deficit and inflation concerns.
An appeals court on Thursday upheld a block on Trump’s executive order limiting mail voting. The Supreme Court is already considering the same case, reflecting the frenzied legal rush as states are send out mail ballots for the midterm elections. The plan would prohibit the Postal Service from delivering mail ballots from states that don’t get pre-approval for envelope design and submit a list of voters.
Trump also said Wednesday that oil prices that have surged because of the Iran war likely won’t come down until after U.S. midterm elections. The comments were a striking acknowledgment from Trump about the conflict as his Republican administration faces mounting pressure to address high gas prices as the war in Iran grinds on with no conclusion in sight.
Here's the latest:
Some protesters march near GOP convention site
With chants of “say it loud, say it clear, Donald Trump’s not welcome here,” the demonstrators marched Thursday down streets near the American Airlines Center.
But before the protesters could get too close to the site of the Republican’s midterm convention, police stopped them. There’s been a heavy security presence around the convention venue and many nearby roads are closed.
The group held up signs, including some reading: “Vote Blue” and “I’m Against Trump’s Deportation Agenda.”
A few counterprotesters shadowed the group nearby.
Smithsonian marks 25th anniversary of 9/11 with display of rare artifacts
The Smithsonian’s National Museum of American History is honoring the 25th anniversary of the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks this week with displays of dozens of rarely seen objects that tell the story of that day in often searing personal terms.
Among them are seat belts from doomed United Airlines Flight 93, a purse and wallet recovered from the World Trade Center site, and also the telephone at the desk of then U.S. Solicitor General Ted Olson’ when his wife, Barbara, called from one of the hijacked planes.
The exhibit runs through Saturday, and it comes as the museum is under growing scrutiny by Trump and Republicans in Congress over the manner in which it tells American history.
Trump meets with Medal of Honor recipients
The president met with recipients of the highest military honor on Thursday during a visit to the National Medal of Honor Museum.
President Trump called the site “an American treasure dedicated to the best and bravest warriors in our country.”
After meeting with military veterans and giving remarks, Trump signed a new bill calling for the creation of a Medal of Honor monument on the National Mall in Washington. The bipartisan bill cleared Congress in August.
Trump stopped by the museum in Arlington, Texas, between events at the Republican midterm convention underway in Dallas. The museum opened last year and honors the more than 3,500 service members who received the award.
Senate majority leader headlines fundraiser for Ken Paxton, Texas Senate candidate
Senate Majority Leader John Thune headlined a fundraiser for Texas Republican Senate nominee Ken Paxton in Dallas on Thursday.
The move is intended to help the candidate he and other Senate leadership opposed to be the GOP’s 2026 standard-bearer in the state. The event was confirmed by a Republican familiar with the event who was not permitted to discuss it because it was a private event.
It was unclear how much money Paxton was expected to raise from Thursday’s event. But he has trailed markedly in fundraising with Democratic Senate nominee James Talarico in the campaign’s final weeks.
Speaking Wednesday to the Republican Midterm Convention in Dallas, Paxton made his own fundraising pitch to those watching on TV, telling them, “I need your prayers, your votes and your support.”
House Democrats say they’re about more than just criticizing Trump
U.S. Rep. Sydney Kamlager-Dove said working-class struggles in her Los Angeles district keep her focused on more than just blasting the president.
She said Thursday in Dallas that fellow Democrats “have an action recovery plan for the American people, and we are 100% committed to ... bring the cost of living down.”
Jason Crow, her House colleague from Colorado, said it’s time “to stop the bleeding.”
He said House Democrats, if they gain the majority in the chamber, would be able to put a check on Trump’s trade wars, reverse Republicans’ Medicaid cuts and take other actions in support of their positions.
Even if a Democratic House majority could not get legislation signed by the Republican Trump, there’s another key role Democrats say they could play: oversight of the president and his administration.
The delegation in Dallas said it plans to dig into the Trump family’s business dealings and examine how they’ve seen their wealth climb significantly since the president’s return to the White House.
“We will have both the power of the purse and the power of the gavel,” said Kamlager-Dove.
Canada’s prime minister says he and Trump have spoken even as their trade war escalates
The Canadian prime minister, Mark Carney said Thursday that the conversations with Trump occurred in “recent days” and involved Ukraine, Iran and other global developments.
“We continue to have work with the United States. We can compartmentalize across this,” Carney said. The contact comes after another escalation in the U.S.-Canada trade war.
Washington this week banned some Canadian alcoholic beverages and some dairy products and motorcycles after Canadian retaliatory tariffs took effect on about $20 billion in U.S. goods. Trump also moved to exclude Canadian products from large, long-term U.S. government contracts.
Trade talks collapsed last month, but Carney said Canada remains open to an agreement.
“Canada is always ready to strike a fair deal,” he said.
Missouri election officials ordered to use 2022 congressional map in November
Missouri’s Republican secretary of state Denny Hoskins has ordered local election authorities to use the 2022 congressional map instead of a congressional map backed by President Donald Trump.
Hoskins announced the change in a statement following a decision Thursday by the U.S. Supreme Court rejecting the map backed by Trump. The map favored by Trump was drawn in a bid to help Republicans gain an additional U.S. House seat. But that has led to weeks of legal wrangling.
It’s all part of a pitched court battle that has created confusion for voters and others shortly before ballots begin going out for the November elections.
Vice President Vance raises $2M on the sidelines of the Republicans' Dallas convention
The vice president, who also serves as the Republican National Committee’s finance chair, brought in a big haul for the party on Thursday at a fundraiser in Dallas. That’s according to a person familiar with the event who was not authorized to speak publicly.
JD Vance has been raising millions for the party since last year in the role.
The position also puts him front of the GOP’s key donors who could be vital if he launches a 2028 presidential campaign.
House Democrats descend on Dallas to blast Trump’s two-day ‘party’
Leading House Democrats are in Texas blasting the Republicans’ midterm convention as an opulent spectacle for an out-of-touch president.
“As Donald Trump and J.D. Vance party away for two days, the average American family can’t afford the groceries,” said Democratic Rep. Robert Garcia of California. “Donald Trump does not care about the average American family or about affordability.”
That has been a theme of Democratic responses this week.
The Democrats have been juxtaposing big donors paying for access to Trump with rising prices of fuel, groceries and other consumer goods.
“We’re the Truth Brigade, and the American people are tired of the lies,” said Rep. Sydney Kamlager-Dove, another California Democrat.
Democratic U.S. Rep Jason Crow of Colorado said Trump’s midterm convention is a “fantasy land” that is especially offensive now that the U.S. is six months into the president’s war in Iran. Crow is a military veteran, having served in Iraq and Afghanistan as an Army officer.
Voting and civil rights groups sue to keep ICE away from polls
The lawsuit cites a statute dating back to the Civil War that forbids armed federal officers from approaching voting sites. It says that law conflicts with Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin’s statement earlier this month that ICE Agents could appear at polls in November in response to specific threats or while pursuing suspects.
The groups, and the city of Denver, which also joined the suit, ask that a federal judge in Washington forbid the department from sending agents to polling places.
Democrats have long worried that Trump will send ICE to polls to try to scare voters away in November. Several Trump administration officials have denied this would happen, though some of the president’s allies have openly called for him to take that step.
Trump administration silence has 200,000 Salvadoran immigrants hoping they’re protected
A deadline for the Trump administration to decide whether about 200,000 immigrants from El Salvador can remain protected from deportation has passed without any public announcement, raising hopes among many for another six-month extension while also sowing confusion.
The Department of Homeland Security has been quiet about its plans, leaving attorneys and advocates scrambling to decipher what might happen next to Salvadorans who’ve been raising families in the U.S. for decades.
On Thursday, Homeland Security issued a statement saying the department would make an announcement “at an appropriate time” and that Temporary Protected Status for El Salvador would stay in effect until then. The department issued the same statement during Wednesday’s deadline.
“Let’s be clear: this is not an official extension or decision by DHS as to the fate of TPS for El Salvador,” Ben Johnson, who directs the American Immigration Lawyers Association, posted Wednesday on social media. The Trump administration is leaving TPS holders, their families and their employers in limbo, he said.
▶ Read more
Trump promises $500 Obamacare rebate checks for 1M enrollees in 30 states
It would be for those whom the White House alleges were overcharged by the Biden administration for exchange fees.
The promise comes after Trump pledged Wednesday to send every American adult $5,000 if Republicans retain control of the House and Senate in the midterm elections and as affordability has become a central issue for voters heading into November.
“The relief begins with refunding everyone who was overcharged and the rebates are going out in just a few weeks,” Trump said in a recorded address released on the White House X account Thursday.
In a fact sheet, the White House claimed former President Joe Biden’s administration “accumulated a significant surplus of funds that were not used to benefit the Americans who paid these higher premiums.”
It’s unclear where the money for the rebates would come from and whether it requires congressional approval for disbursement.
▶ Read more
US Supreme Court decision appears to clear the way for Missouri to use the old map
There were no noted dissents in the brief order.
It comes after a pitched court battle shortly before ballots begin going out for the November elections. The new map was drawn to help Republicans gain an additional seat.
The Supreme Court order came hours after a federal judge allowed Missouri’s top court to proceed with a contempt hearing against Republican Secretary of State Denny Hoskins. Missouri’s battle over its congressional districts has spanned more than a year and spawned confusion over which districts will be in place for voters.
US Supreme Court again rejects push to use Trump-backed congressional map in Missouri
The U.S. Supreme Court again rejected a push to use Missouri congressional maps backed by President Trump on Thursday, a loss for Republicans trying to maintain control of the House in the fast-approaching midterm elections.
The decision appears to clear the way for use of the old maps.
It comes after a pitched court battle shortly before ballots begin going out for the pivotal November elections. The maps were drawn to help Republicans gain an additional U.S. House seat.
It’s the second time the high court has refused to intervene to keep the Trump-backed maps in place.
▶ Read more
‘Dividend’ is the latest in a long tradition of presidents taking branding liberties
Trump’s “dividend” payments wouldn’t be true dividends. But he’s not the first politician to use labels that stretch the realities of certain policies.
Franklin Roosevelt called Social Security an “old-age insurance system.” But insurance involves premium payments from policy holders financing claims to those same customers. In Social Security, existing workers’ taxes are immediately paid out to older beneficiaries.
Barack Obama pitched his 2009 economic “stimulus bill.” Most of it was tax cuts and direct aid to state governments after the 2008 financial crash. It was more a stabilizing effort than a stimulus.
Republicans call the estate tax, adopted under Democrat Woodrow Wilson, the “death tax” and often suggest it applies broadly. The current exemption is $15 million ($30 million per couple), meaning only inheritances above that are assessed. The Center on Budget and Policy Priorities estimates that fewer than 1 out of 1,000 deaths yield any federal estate tax.
Jump in oil prices comes as hopes fade that US and Iran may reach a deal soon on Strait of Hormuz
That would fully reopen the strait and allow oil tankers to freely exit the Persian Gulf. President Trump said Wednesday that oil prices likely won’t come down until after the U.S. midterm elections in November.
The jump has pushed the price of a gallon of regular gasoline to an average of nearly $4.28 across the United States, according to AAA. That’s up nearly 34% from a year earlier and is not only costing people more at the pump but also through higher prices for all kinds of products that move by truck to store shelves.
Trump’s chosen ‘dividend’ branding doesn’t fit the usual definition
Investopedia, a leading online source of information about the financial markets, defines “dividends” as “periodic payments made to shareholders from corporate profits.”
That doesn’t apply to direct payments or indirect payments (such as tax credits) from the U.S. Treasury Department to taxpayers. The government is not a for-profit enterprise. Furthermore, the treasury has run an annual deficit every year since 2002 — the first fiscal year following President George W. Bush’s first tax cuts. Since there’s no surplus to divide, that means any payouts would have to be backed by debt instruments that would add to the federal operating deficit and total debt.
The current year’s deficit stands at about $1.8 trillion. The total debt surpassed $40 trillion earlier this year.
Investopedia, meanwhile, also says this about dividend payments: “They can make a stock more attractive to investors but may also signal that a company isn’t doing enough to generate better returns.”
Republicans showcase their ‘big beautiful bill’ to voters, but the law’s impact has been mixed
Working to keep the majority in Congress, Republicans at the midterm convention in Dallas are showcasing their chief legislative accomplishment — the sweeping package of tax breaks, social service cuts and immigration enforcement President Trump signed into law.
A year on, what’s known as the One Big Beautiful Bill — or, the “Big Ugly Bill,” as Democrats call it — has produced mixed results. Millions of people have received enhanced tax breaks, while millions are also losing access to federal food aid and health care. More immigrants are being arrested, many deported, some dying during the process.
House Speaker Mike Johnson calls it the kind of “common sense” governing that Republicans plan to do more of, if voters return them to power.
“Shamefully, not one Democrat voted for it,” Rep. Derrick Van Orden, R-Wis., said Wednesday during the convention’s opening night.
▶ Read more
One Republican senator seems to like Trump’s ‘dividend’ idea
Kansas Sen. Roger Marshall, who’s attending the GOP midterm convention as he seeks his second term, is among the Republicans embracing Trump’s proposed payout to American adults.
“Comment how you will spend your $5,000 Trump Dividend when Republicans win in November,” he posted on X, eliciting mostly positive responses from his online followers.
Kansas has not elected a Democrat to the U.S. Senate since the 1932 wave election in the Great Depression. But Marshall faces a surprisingly energetic challenge for reelection from Democratic nominee Adam Hamilton, pastor of the nation’s largest United Methodist congregation.
Marshall did not expound on the cost of Trump’s idea or how it should be carried out legally. The president doesn’t have appropriations power under the Constitution. That power rests with Congress.
US oil jumps above $100 and stock futures slump
The price of U.S. crude oil rose above $100 for the first time Thursday since May with no end in sight in the U.S.-Iran war.
The price for Brent crude, the international standard, rose above $105 a barrel. U.S. stock futures fell, with the S&P 500 down 0.5% and the Nasdaq off by 1.1%.
A report showed that inflation in the U.S. remains stubbornly high on the wholesale level.
Meanwhile, the European Central Bank raised its key interest rate by one-quarter point to try to tame inflation in the European Union. Stock indexes in Europe fell, with Germany’s DAX down 0.7%.
Market in Asia closed lower with the exception of Japan.
▶ Read more
Americans’ individual share of the US debt payments equals 3/4 of Trump’s ‘dividend’ payment
The theoretical $5,000 payments Trump pitched would mean money going directly in Americans’ wallets. But Americans’ also are on the hook for an indirect outlay that’s almost as much: interest payments on the U.S. debt.
The national debt recently crossed the $40 trillion mark. Each year, the federal government pays interest to the investors who’ve financed that debt.
According to Treasury Department data, that interest expense for fiscal year 2026 will come to about $1.27 trillion. Using the Census Bureau’s 2026 population estimate of 340.3 million people, that comes to a per capita share of $3,732 or almost three-quarters of the payout Trump pitched.
Federal judge allows contempt hearing in Missouri redistricting dispute
A federal judge has allowed Missouri’s top court to proceed with a contempt hearing Thursday for Republican Secretary of State Denny Hoskins in a tense and twisting legal battle over whether new congressional districts supported by President Trump can be used in the November election.
Missouri’s top court previously ordered Hoskins not to use a Trump-backed map in the general election. But U.S. District Judge Stephen Clark on Tuesday barred Hoskins from using anything other than the new map Trump supports.
The state Supreme Court then ordered Hoskins to appear for a contempt hearing Thursday for not following its orders.
State attorneys representing Hoskins had asked Clark to halt the contempt hearing. But Clark declined to do so.
▶ Read more
GOP donor doesn’t like Trump’s proposed $5,000 checks
Joe Lonsdale, a prominent Republican donor and activist, is among the Trump allies panning the president’s latest promise to send money directly to Americans.
“I am hugely in favor of winning the midterms, and love much about this (administration),” he wrote on X, “but am strongly against bread and circus bribes.”
Democrats say Trump’s ‘bizarre’ convention is a distraction from his faltering presidency
It’s not just Republicans descending on Dallas for the midterm convention — Democrats are there too as they try to convince voters that the reality of Donald Trump’s second presidency doesn’t match the spectacle of his made-for-TV event.
“This bizarre Republican midterm convention here can’t paper over the fact that Republicans have done nothing to earn your vote,” Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker, a potential 2028 presidential contender, said Wednesday morning.
Besides Pritzker, several leading House Democrats were traveling to Dallas for events, as well. And Texas Democrats hope the spotlight on the state ends up benefiting their candidates.
James Talarico, a Texas state lawmaker who's running against state Attorney General Ken Paxton in a closely watched Senate race, held a food drive Wednesday at Friendship West Baptist Church in Dallas. He compared volunteers’ work with Republicans’ festivities.
▶ Read more
Trump says oil prices that spiked because of Iran war likely won’t come down until after midterms
Trump said Wednesday that oil prices that have surged because of the Iran war likely won’t come down until after U.S. midterm elections.
Oil prices on Wednesday jumped more than 3%, pushing international Brent crude past the $100 threshold for the first time since July as salvos between the U.S. and Iran escalated.
“Right after the election, oil prices are going to be tumbling downward,” Trump said. “I think it’s going to take a little bit longer than the midterm.”
The comments were a striking acknowledgment from Trump about the conflict as his Republican administration faces mounting pressure to address high gas prices as the war in Iran grinds on with no conclusion in sight.
Trump, in an exchange with reporters before traveling to Dallas for the midterm Republican convention, added that he believes Iran will finally relent after the pivotal elections are held in the U.S.
▶ Read more
Trump, hoping to salvage midterms, makes dubious pledge to give every US adult $5,000 if GOP wins
President Donald Trump pledged Wednesday to send every American adult $5,000 if Republicans retain control of the House and Senate in the midterm elections, an extraordinary gambit to reverse his party’s sagging fortunes in November.
The dubious promise would likely cost more than $1 trillion and require congressional approval, and would further exacerbate the country’s nearly $1.8 trillion annual budget deficit and concerns about inflation.
“If the Republicans win, you win with us and you get $5,000,” Trump said during the GOP’s midterm convention in Dallas. “It will be called the Trump Dividend.”
He likened the payments to a corporation’s distributions to shareholders, citing “our tremendous strength and success economically.”
Within an hour, Vice President JD Vance appeared to try to walk back Trump’s proposal — at least in part — by suggesting the dividend payments would not go to the wealthy. Vance suggested it could be paid for by U.S. tariff revenues, though the suggested payment dwarfs what the U.S. has taken in through the protectionist measures.

sources.news_title: Supreme Court Blocks GOP Attempt to Steal Seats in Missouri—for Now
sources.text:
Supreme Court Shockingly Blocks Republican Maps in Red State
The high court just threw the state’s midterm elections into chaos.
Jamie Squire/Getty Images
The Supreme Court has blocked a federal judge’s decision about Missouri’s voting map, further throwing the state’s election into chaos.
The nation’s highest judiciary issued an order in the pending case Thursday, directing the state to rely on the original congressional maps that were drawn after the 2020 census during the upcoming midterm cycle, rather than the 2025 map created at Donald Trump’s behest, which would have granted Republicans an extra seat in the House.
It’s possible that this won’t be the Supreme Court’s final say on the matter, however. The legal memo noted that the stay will remain in place unless the case (People Not Politicians v. Onder) receives a final ruling, either by being elevated to the court’s bench or by being referred back to a lower court.
The drama began last summer, when Trump ordered several Republican-led states to redraw their congressional maps in a brazen attempt to create a GOP advantage in Washington.
Congressional maps are typically redrawn every 10 years, in accordance with the census cycle, allowing states to more accurately reflect changing local populations and meet their respective political needs. Yet Trump’s order arrived in the middle of the decade, raising alarms that the nationwide effort was an attempt to undermine U.S. democracy.
Republicans wasted no time implementing the directive in Missouri, where they shaved portions off a Democratic stronghold encompassing Kansas City, endangering Representative Emanuel Cleaver’s seat. The new map offered Republicans a 7–1 advantage, a one-seat gain over their previous 6–2 delegation.
A group called People Not Politicians collected more than 300,000 signatures in opposition to the new map—more than double the amount required—to force a statewide referendum on the matter, which is due to take place on November 3 on the statewide ballot.
Regardless, Missouri pushed ahead, opting to use the new maps during its August 4 primary. But this week, things got especially messy.
A federal judge ruled on Tuesday that the state should use the new maps during the November election, in light of the primary using the new districts. But that judge’s decision was in direct conflict with an order from Supreme Court Justice Brett Kavanaugh, who had decided moments earlier that another legal decision on the matter—the Missouri Supreme Court overturning the new map—should stand. In doing so, Kavanaugh effectively decided that Missouri should use its original maps, rather than the new one drafted last year.
The Supreme Court’s Thursday decision raises more questions about how the midterm election will be carried out, given how primary votes were conducted.
Trump Brags About Convention Crowd Size to Half-Empty Room
Multiple videos reveal that the crowd was not what Donald Trump promised it would be.
People listen to Donald Trump speak at the Republican midterm convention.
Brandon Bell/Getty Images
People listen to Donald Trump speak at the Republican midterm convention.
“Trump-a-palooza” is off to a disastrous start.
President Donald Trump promised that the Republican Party’s midterm convention would be “sold out” Wednesday—but hours into the opening day, there were still hundreds of empty seats at the American Airlines Center outside of Dallas.
“This place is packed. And not only is this packed, it’s a big arena, not only is this packed, but you have an equal number of people standing outside,” Trump told the arena.
Trump continued to self-consciously ramble about the size of his audience throughout his address.
“This is our big room. This place is packed,” Trump said. “Do you think the fake news, you know what they’re gonna do? The fake news will go around and see that man up there? He’s leaving for the bathroom. He’ll be back in two minutes. Up in the—they’ll take a picture of his seat while he’s gone. And they’ll say, ‘Trump did not fill up the arena. The arena was not filled.’”
An hour later, Trump returned to the subject. “They’ll have a reporter say, ‘Trump lost his audience. He didn’t enjoy it up there.’ I do. I’m having a lot of fun. You know why? Cause everybody loves me, and I love everybody,” Trump said.
Shortly before Trump was scheduled to give his keynote address, House Speaker Mike Johnson told NewsMax’s Finnerty that the arena was full—even as the camera panned over dozens of empty seats.
“Yeah, it’s full. I’m looking around, I think every seat up to the rafters are full,” Johnson said.
PBS News’s Liz Landers posted a video on X of the convention “kicking off” earlier that evening. The video showed that most of the 20,000-seat basketball arena was still empty, with just a few hundred attendees sitting on the floor and lower levels.
“Capacity-wise they could have held this in a high school gym,” former Democratic staffer Aaron Fritschner wrote on X.
Later, another video posted by a Minnesota state Republican representative showed that the entire upper deck of the convention center was empty. Attendees witnessed one convention organizer running through the halls encouraging people to sit in the still-empty sections, The Daily Beast reported.
Minnesota Republican state representative posts video from Trumpapalooza showing that the whole upper deck is empty pic.twitter.com/wm0dSMa9ah
It might’ve been that long waits in the hot Texas sun that attendees were subjected to kept people away.
Alec Shears, a conservative pundit, described the outdoor check-in. “3 people have needed medical attention so far. Several have already gone home,” he wrote on X.
The Texas Observer’s Steven Monacelli observed that there was a heat advisory in Dallas Fort Worth. “I may have overestimated my progress through the line. I’m approaching hour two of waiting in what feels like 100+ heat and I still have not gotten a credential for the GOP midterm gathering in Dallas. One ambulance has already come and gone,” he wrote on X.
Trump Advisers Secretly Issue Dire Warning About Iran War
The odds of a new forever war are looking increasingly likely.
RONALDO SCHEMIDT/AFP/Getty Images
The current conflict against Iran could become another forever war.
White House officials have privately told Donald Trump that the war could last through the end of his term—a stark about-face from the president’s repetitive public messaging on the matter, which has involved tireless promises since February that the war’s end is immediately forthcoming.
Some of Trump’s closest advisers—including Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio—have discussed the conflict’s potentially extended timeline with the president, The Wall Street Journal reported Wednesday. The White House is exploring the possibility that Tehran could continue to resist U.S. pressure, which insiders told the Journal could push the war even beyond Inauguration Day 2029.
Despite the dire reality of the closed-door conversations, Trump has invariably echoed his administration’s forecast for the war to the American public. Speaking with reporters on Wednesday, Trump pledged that the conflict will end “immediately” after the midterm elections in November “because they can’t hold out any longer.”
That drawn-out timeline could spell disaster for American defenses, which have already reached a “beyond critical” missile shortage.
The Iran war has done nothing good for America in the six months since it began. The conflict has so far killed at least 18 U.S. service members and wounded more than 750 others. It has also killed more than 3,500 people in Iran and injured tens of thousands of locals, according to data published by Al Jazeera.
The conflict has also taken an enormous toll on daily life in the U.S., inflaming the cost of practically everything as shipping companies contend with rising oil costs. As a result, Trump’s approval rating has plummeted, with trust and loyalty rattled even amongst his base, who are reportedly losing patience with the unyielding violence.
Even MAGA World Isn’t Buying Trump’s Free Money Promise

sources.text:
Competing Court Orders Add Confusion To Missouri Congressional Elections
JEFFERSON CITY, Mo. (AP) — Dueling court orders eight weeks before Election Day left Missouri’s congressional map uncertain Tuesday as legal wrangling over a redistricting plan backed by President Donald Trump sparked fresh confusion.
A federal judge in Missouri on Tuesday temporarily blocked the state from using its old congressional districts in the November election. But that came just moments after the U.S. Supreme Court let stand a decision from the Missouri Supreme Court ordering the old districts to be used instead of new ones favored by Trump.
The decisions highlight the bewildering nature of Missouri’s redistricting battle, which has spanned more than a year and leaves Missouri voters in some parts of the state uncertain which district they will be in on Election Day.
Missouri's top court ruled last week that the new Trump-backed map cannot be used because citizens turned in thousands of petition signatures demanding a statewide vote on it.
The U.S. Supreme Court declined to take up an appeal from Missouri’s Republican attorney general, leaving in place the injunction from Missouri’s top court. But moments later, U.S. District Judge Stephen Clark, a Trump appointee, issued a temporary restraining order prohibiting Missouri from using anything other than the new districts backed by Republicans.
Redistricting opponents quickly filed a notice to appeal that order to the 8th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals.
The new districts were used in the August primary, and the winners already were certified by election officials. But the question of which districts will be used in the November election continues to linger. Clark's order remains in place for 14 days, allowing time for additional court proceedings.
Missouri Attorney General Catherine Hanaway said the state “is prepared to follow and comply with” Clark's order, which she said “binds the state to using” the new congressional districts.
Republican Secretary of State Denny Hoskins, who oversees elections, described the federal court order as a victory that “halts a full-on constitutional crisis.” He immediately notified local election officials that they are required to use the new districts.
But an attorney for People Not Politicians, the group that sponsored the referendum petition, stressed that the order from Missouri’s top court against using the new map also remains in effect. The group's leader filed a request Tuesday night with the state Supreme Court to hold Hoskins in contempt for attempting to use the new map, and the court scheduled arguments for Thursday on the request.
“An individual federal judge cannot overrule the Missouri Supreme Court,” said attorney Chuck Hatfield, who represents People Not Politicians.
Judge Says Switching Maps Could 'Wreak Havoc'
Hanaway has argued it would violate federal rights and cause confusion to switch districts for voters between the primary and general elections. Clark agreed in his written order.
“Using a different map for the general election would wreak havoc on the fairness and orderliness of Missouri’s congressional elections, calling into question the candidacy of those nominated in the primaries and the votes of those who voted in the primaries," Clark wrote. "Widespread voter confusion would inevitably follow.”
U.S. Supreme Court Justice Brett Kavanaugh, who handles cases from Missouri, did not explain the rationale for declining to take up the case.
Missouri law set a Tuesday deadline to change the candidates or issues on the November ballot. But the determination of which ballots voters receive could take longer. Federal law sets a Sept. 19 deadline to begin mailing absentee ballots to overseas citizens and military members.
New Missouri District Targets Democrat From Kansas City
Missouri currently is represented in the U.S. House by six Republicans and two Democrats who were elected under districts that Republican state officials approved in 2022.
But at Trump’s urging, Missouri Gov. Mike Kehoe called the Legislature into a special session last year to redraw congressional boundaries to Republicans' advantage ahead of the midterms.
The revised map targeted the 5th Congressional District, held by longtime Democratic Rep. Emanuel Cleaver of Kansas City. It reassigned portions of Kansas City to two neighboring districts represented by Republicans and stretched the remainder of Cleaver’s district far eastward into rural Republican areas.
About 59% of the district’s voters were new under the revised map, according to an Associated Press estimate.
Cleaver, who was unopposed in the Democratic primary, praised Tuesday's U.S. Supreme Court action and expressed confidence the old districts will ultimately be used.
State Sen. Rick Brattin won the Republican primary in the reshaped district. He joined with Republican U.S. Rep. Bob Onder and other voters to file the federal lawsuit resulting in Clark's temporary order. Brattin praised that decision while pledging a continued campaign.
Missouri's Top Court Said New Districts Never Became Law
On the same day as the primary, Hoskins rejected a petition with thousands of signatures seeking to force a November referendum on the map. Hoskins asserted that Missouri’s Constitution doesn’t allow a referendum on congressional redistricting. A lower court agreed, but the state Supreme Court reversed Hoskins’ decision.
The state’s top court said the new districts were retroactively frozen in December, when the petition signatures were submitted, and thus never became law. Hoskins on Tuesday assigned the redistricting referendum as Proposition A on the November ballot, in compliance with the state court order.
The Missouri Constitution does not specifically say that a referendum can be used for congressional redistricting. But the state Supreme Court said a constitutional provision allowing a referendum on “any act” of the Legislature encompasses congressional redistricting legislation.
Missouri was the second Republican-led state, after Texas, to respond to Trump’s call last year to redraw congressional districts. Several other states followed. All told, Republicans hoped to win as many as 16 additional seats from new House maps enacted in eight states — Texas, Missouri, North Carolina, Ohio, Florida, Tennessee, Louisiana and Alabama. Democrats, whose counterattack faced several setbacks, think they could win up to six additional seats from new districts in California and Utah.
It remains to be seen whether the redistricting works as intended for Republicans. The president’s party historically has lost congressional seats in the midterms, and Trump’s poor approval ratings could provide an extra hurdle for Republican candidates.

sources.news_title: Supreme Court Blocks Missouri Congressional Map for Midterm Election
sources.text:
Supreme Court Blocks Missouri Congressional Map for Midterm Election
                     
                
                WASHINGTON — The Supreme Court on Thursday stayed a federal court order that would have required Missouri to use a Republican-drawn congressional map in the November midterm election, leaving the state’s existing 2022 district boundaries in place while the legal dispute continues.
The court’s unsigned order, issued without a recorded dissent or explanation, struck down an order from a federal judge in St. Louis that had required election officials to use the new map, known as HB 1.
The map was expected to improve Republican chances of winning a congressional seat now held by a Democrat.
The ruling resolved an immediate conflict between state and federal courts. The Missouri Supreme Court had ordered officials to use the 2022 map until voters decide whether to approve the new boundaries in a statewide referendum.
The referendum is scheduled for the November ballot. Its outcome could determine whether the Republican-backed map takes effect in later elections.
The case, People Not Politicians v. Onder, reached the Supreme Court after federal and state rulings issued within days of one another produced uncertainty over which districts would govern the general election.
U.S. District Judge Stephen Clark had ruled that returning to the 2022 map after Missouri conducted its August primary under the new boundaries could violate constitutional protections.
He said voters could be required to cast general-election ballots in districts with different candidates from those used in the primary.
Missouri Attorney General Catherine Hanaway, a Republican, argued in court filings that changing the map would disrupt preparations for the election, require officials to revise ballots and potentially disenfranchise hundreds of thousands of voters who participated in the primary.
The organizers of the referendum challenged the federal order, saying the state court’s ruling was controlling and that the new map could not take effect before voters had an opportunity to approve it.
They also argued that the federal order had injected further confusion into the election process.
The Supreme Court’s action came after Justice Brett Kavanaugh earlier declined to block the Missouri Supreme Court’s order in a separate case.
Kavanaugh handles emergency applications from Missouri but referred the latest dispute to the full court.
Richard von Glahn, who leads People Not Politicians, said the decision would allow Missouri voters to decide the fate of the new map. The group says more than 300,000 voters signed petitions seeking the referendum.
Supporters of the new map, including state Republican officials, have said the boundaries are lawful and necessary to reflect Missouri’s political makeup.
The map was approved by the Republican-controlled Legislature last year after President Donald Trump urged Republican-led states to consider redistricting before the 2026 elections.
Kansas City Mayor Quinton Lucas said in a statement that the ruling was a victory for Missouri voters and the referendum process. He criticized state officials for creating uncertainty over which map would govern the election.
The competing court orders had prompted emergency filings, instructions to local election officials and a scheduled contempt hearing involving Secretary of State Denny Hoskins. State election officials had warned that deadlines for finalizing ballots and sending mail ballots were approaching.
The Supreme Court did not decide the underlying legal questions surrounding the referendum or permanently determine which map will govern future elections. The federal litigation remains pending.

sources.text:
Supreme Court blocks Republican-favored Missouri election map, ending legal whiplash
(WASHINGTON) -- The Supreme Court has blocked Missouri Republicans from moving forward with a U.S. House map that the state's highest court had already invalidated ahead of the November election.
In a brief unexplained order, and over no noted dissent by any justices, the court granted a request by a Democrat-backed advocacy group to pause a lower federal court order that greenlit the GOP-favored map just days ago.
The decision likely ends the legal whiplash over Missouri's map two months before the high-stakes midterm election takes place. It also hands Democrats a small victory in the nationwide mid-decade redistricting war.
State Republicans could still technically attempt to ask the justices to take the case for oral argument and decide the merits, but that process would very likely exceed the time left before the vote -- and the Democratic-favored map would remain in effect in the meantime, the order indicated.
State election officials will now bear the brunt of having to quickly lay groundwork for administering the vote with a district map different from the one used in the primary.
The group that sought to preserve the 2022 map calls this the "definitive answer" in Missouri for November.
"The law is the law, the Missouri constitution is clear as was the Missouri Supreme Court," Richard von Glahn, executive director of the group pushing the referendum vote, People Not Politicians, said in a statement. "Over 305,000 Missouri voters -- Republicans, Democrats and Independents took action to block this political power grab last fall. People, not politicians, will have the final say when they vote NO on Proposition A this November."
The state's Republican-controlled legislature last year passed into law a new congressional map that redrew the district currently held by Democratic Rep. Emanuel Cleaver to lean Republican as part of a nationwide mid-decade redistricting push encouraged by President Donald Trump.
But Democrats and other opponents of the new map filed legal challenges, pushing for a ballot initiative to put the new map up for a vote in November. They also argued that if the new map was put up for a referendum vote in November, that would suspend the law establishing the new map unless voters approved it and that Missouri's elections should be held under the state's older congressional map.
Missouri Secretary of State Denny Hoskins initially decided in early August that he would not certify the referendum to the ballot, saying he had determined it was unconstitutional. People Not Politicians successfully appealed that ruling to the state Supreme Court, which ruled to block the new map from being used in November and to allow the ballot initiative to proceed.
Republicans appealed to the U.S. Supreme Court seeking intervention as they simultaneously pursued a second-track legal front.
Just days ago, Supreme Court Justice Brett Kavanaugh, who oversees Missouri federal courts, declined to intervene in the dispute over Missouri's congressional map.
Earlier this month, a federal district court judge directed the state to use the GOP-favored map, which was used in the primary, even though the state's highest court directed the opposite.
Missouri Republicans had pushed back against a change to the map, saying in a court filing that a change-up at this late hour would "disenfranchise millions of primary voters" and "unilaterally void a congressional map before a statewide vote."

sources.news_title: Supreme Court Halts Missouri’s GOP-Backed Congressional Map Ahead of November Election
sources.text:
The U.S. Supreme Court on Thursday blocked Missouri from using a newly drawn congressional map in November’s midterm elections, at least temporarily preventing the state from implementing district lines that could have given Republicans control of seven of Missouri’s eight House seats.
In a brief order with no noted dissents, the justices granted an emergency request to stay a federal court ruling that had required election officials to use the new map. The order leaves the Republican-backed map on hold while the litigation over Missouri’s congressional districts continues.
Unless another court ruling changes the situation, Missouri will conduct the November election using the congressional boundaries adopted following the 2020 census. Under those lines, the state’s current House delegation consists of six Republicans and two Democrats.
The disputed map, approved by Missouri lawmakers in 2025, substantially reshaped portions of Kansas City in a way that made the 5th Congressional District, represented by Rep. Emanuel Cleaver, a Democrat, more favorable to Republicans. Had the map been used, the St. Louis-area 1st District represented by Democratic Rep. Wesley Bell could have been the only Democratic-held congressional seat in the state.
Thursday’s Supreme Court intervention came after an unusual series of conflicting state and federal court decisions over which map Missouri should use in the rapidly approaching election.
Last week, the Missouri Supreme Court ruled that opponents of the new map had validly invoked the state Constitution’s referendum process after collecting the required signatures. The court ordered Secretary of State Denny Hoskins to place the map before voters on the November ballot and prohibited state officials from using the new districts unless voters approve them.
The state’s high court concluded that the referendum petition was timely and legally valid and that the Missouri Constitution permits voters to challenge congressional redistricting legislation through the referendum process. Under its ruling, the congressional districts established in 2022 were to remain in effect for the November election.
The dispute took another turn Tuesday when U.S. District Judge Stephen Clark in St. Louis issued a temporary restraining order requiring Hoskins to use the newly drawn map rather than the older district lines. That federal ruling came shortly after Supreme Court Justice Brett Kavanaugh had declined a separate request from Missouri officials to interfere with the Missouri Supreme Court’s decision.
Opponents of the new districts then returned to the U.S. Supreme Court, asking the justices to suspend Clark’s order. Thursday’s ruling granted that request, once again putting the newer congressional map on hold as the broader legal battle continues.

U.S. Supreme Court deals Missouri GOP another blow in congressional map fight
What do you think?
The U.S. Supreme Court on Thursday again rejected an effort to use Missouri’s Republican-drawn 2025 congressional map in the Nov. 3 election, delivering another setback to Republicans trying to gain an additional U.S. House seat.
The decision came in People Not Politicians v. Onder, the latest emergency appeal in a rapidly escalating legal fight that has produced conflicting orders from state and federal courts.
The disputed map was approved by Missouri lawmakers last year after President Donald Trump urged Republican-controlled states to redraw congressional districts ahead of the midterm elections. The new lines were designed to make a Kansas City-area district held by Democratic U.S. Rep. Emanuel Cleaver more favorable to Republicans.
Opponents collected more than 300,000 signatures seeking a statewide referendum on the map.
The Missouri Supreme Court ruled last week that the referendum was valid and ordered Secretary of State Denny Hoskins not to use the 2025 districts unless voters approve them in November. The court ordered Missouri to use its previous congressional districts for the general election.
But the dispute became more complicated this week when Chief U.S. District Judge Stephen Clark issued a conflicting federal order directing Hoskins to use the 2025 map. The 8th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals declined to halt Clark’s order, sending opponents back to the U.S. Supreme Court.
Thursday’s Supreme Court action rejects that latest attempt to preserve the federal ruling requiring use of the new map and appears to clear the way for Missouri to return to its previous congressional districts for the Nov. 3 election.
The decision also comes as Hoskins faces a separate confrontation with the Missouri Supreme Court.
Hoskins was ordered to personally appear before the court Thursday morning and explain why he should not be held in contempt after continuing to direct election officials to use the 2025 map despite the state court’s order.
The confrontation has prompted some Republican state lawmakers to threaten impeachment proceedings against Missouri Supreme Court justices if Hoskins is held in contempt.
The stakes extend beyond Missouri. Republicans currently hold a narrow majority in the U.S. House, and the 2025 Missouri map was drawn with the potential to give the GOP seven of the state’s eight congressional seats.
Missouri voters are still expected to vote on the 2025 redistricting plan in November. If voters approve it, the map could take effect afterward.
For the Nov. 3 congressional election, however, Thursday’s Supreme Court action represents a major victory for opponents of the new districts and another major blow to the Republican redistricting effort.
